Subject: Performance SLO qualification call recap

Hi Jordan — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side based on the discovery: 

- Priority SLOs you called out:
  • Latency: target p95 for user-perceived response (end-to-end) — you said sub-250ms is ideal for the UI flows, 500ms is maximum acceptable for larger responses.
  • Throughput / concurrency: expected steady-state concurrency ~50 concurrent sessions, occasional peaks to 150.
  • Streaming: yes, streaming is important for the primary chat UX (progressive tokens).
  • Context window: typical user input + history ~ 800–1,200 input tokens; average model output ~300–600 tokens; some long workflows may push to ~2,000 input tokens + outputs.

Key unknowns we flagged we want to confirm: typical token distribution (percentile), acceptable degradation modes (e.g., truncate vs. degrade quality), and whether some endpoints can tolerate higher latency to save cost.

Next steps (proposed):
1) You confirm priorities above and share a small sample of payloads (anonymized) and a target percentiles breakdown (p50/p90/p95 input size and output size).
2) We run an initial latency matrix (varied context window sizes + streaming enabled) against a matched model profile and share results + recommended config (batching / quantization / KV cache strategy).
3) Align on a short MUTUAL ACTION PLAN and timing — goal: produce test results within 5 business days after sample payloads arrive.

Attaching: SLO_worksheet.xlsx (fills in the matrix we discussed) and latency_test_results_template.csv.

If the summary looks right, I’ll kick off the test plan with engineering (David) once you send samples.

Thanks,

Thanks for sending this, Jordan — useful sample set. A few engineering notes on the latency/context-window tradeoffs (quick, high-level):

- Context window is directly correlated with per-request compute and memory pressure. For autoregressive models, doubling the context length roughly doubles the attention compute for the generation step; this increases per-token latency.
- Streaming helps the user experience for time-to-first-token, but it does not remove the compute cost of processing long inputs (you still need to encode the full input in most model architectures unless you chunk/hybridize).
- Concurrency at the scale you quoted (50 steady, peaks 150) means we should avoid aggressive single-request batching that would increase p95 latency; instead we recommend continuous batching with small max batch sizes and per-route latency SLOs.
- Options to reduce latency impact: 1) enforce a max input token limit at the API layer with a truncation policy for non-critical history; 2) use KV caching for repeated contexts; 3) use a quantized model variant for lower p95 but verify quality regressions; 4) progressive chunking + streaming for extremely long inputs (process chunks and stream partial outputs).

Action items for us (Redwood engineering) if FinCo confirms priorities:
- Run a latency matrix: models X quantization levels X context windows (512 / 1024 / 2048 / 4096) with streaming enabled/disabled and report p50/p90/p95 token latencies and end-to-end time-to-first-token.
- Use the payload_samples.jsonl as the input distribution and run with concurrency profiles (50, 150).

Jordan — can you confirm the percentile distribution you provided above (p50/p90/p95 for input/output) and whether truncation is acceptable on older history? If truncation is a no-go, we’ll add progressive chunking to the test matrix.

-David
